content: 1. The undersigned agrees not to disclose the discussions and decisions made during JMPS (Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications) meetings to individuals outside these meetings unless explicitly approved by FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) and WHO (World Health Organization). 2. The obligations of the undersigned will remain in effect even after their responsibilities with JMPS have ended. 3. The undersigned agrees to promptly return all copies of any information provided by FAO and/or WHO, depending on the source of the information, upon completion of the JMPS review. 4. Nothing in this agreement or related documents shall be interpreted as a waiver of the privileges and immunities of FAO and/or WHO. (Note: Temporary advisors or experts on mission are entitled to certain privileges and immunities.) 5. Any disputes regarding the interpretation or application of this agreement, unless resolved amicably, will be subject to conciliation under the Conciliation Rules of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) currently in force. If conciliation fails, the dispute will be resolved through arbitration, conducted in accordance with the Arbitration Rules of UNCITRAL. The parties agree to accept the arbitration award as the final resolution of the dispute. 6. A letter of access to confidential data is required during the development of FAO/WHO pesticide specifications. 7. The purpose of the letter of access, provided by the company, is to allow the evaluator (appointed by FAO, WHO, or both) and the registration authority to assess the similarity of the confidential data. The company must include full contact details, including email and postal address, of the contact person and the national authority. 8. The calculations used by WHO/PCS (Pesticide Control System) to advise JMPS are based on known concentrations of the active ingredient and impurities in the technical material, as well as their toxicities (e.g., LD50, ADI, BMD, NOAEL, LOAEL). 9. The maximal acceptable concentration of an impurity in the technical material (TC) is calculated based on a negligible increase in toxicity (10%). If multiple impurities are relevant, their total acceptable concentrations are calculated using their relative toxicities. 10. Examples of impurity relevance are provided: Example 1: An impurity with an acute oral LD50 of 100 mg/kg and a technical material LD50 of 1000 mg/kg has a maximal acceptable impurity concentration of 10 g/kg. If the manufacturing QC limit exceeds 10% of this value, the impurity is considered relevant. Example 2: A biological pesticide with a minimum purity of 200 g/kg and an impurity LD50 of 2000 mg/kg has a maximal acceptable impurity concentration of 200 g/kg. If the QC limit equals 10% of this value, the impurity is relevant. Example 3: An impurity with an LD50 of 400 mg/kg and a technical material LD50 of 600 mg/kg has a maximal acceptable impurity concentration of 70 g/kg. If the QC limit is less than 10% of this value, the impurity is not relevant. 11. Solid mixtures cannot be perfectly blended, and the dispersion of analytical results depends on the size of the test portion analyzed. Therefore, the test portion size must be defined in the specification for a blend of solids. Expanded tolerances for blends are empirically calculated based on achievable manufacturing, sampling, and analytical variations. 12. In 2001, FAO and WHO agreed to jointly develop pesticide specifications, providing robust and universally applicable standards for pesticide quality. This collaboration is based on a Memorandum of Understanding between the two organizations. 13. The March 2016 revision of the first edition of the manual on the development and use of FAO and WHO pesticide specifications supersedes previous versions. It provides standardized processes, unified requirements, harmonized definitions, and technical guidelines applicable to pesticides used in agriculture and public health. 14. FAO/WHO specifications apply only to products from manufacturers whose technical materials have been evaluated. These specifications serve as an international reference for judging product quality, aiding regulatory purposes and commercial dealings, and preventing the trade and use of inferior pesticide products. 15. These specifications enhance confidence in pesticide purchase and use, contributing to improved pest control, sound agricultural production, effective vector control, and better safety for users, the public, and the environment, particularly in developing countries.
